title: Communication With Clients Standard
summary: Every therapist is expected to communicate in a way that makes clients feel welcomed, heard, understood, respected, comfortable, safe, and professionally cared for.

sections.title: The Standard
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, every therapist is expected to communicate with clients in a way that makes them feel welcomed, heard, understood, respected, comfortable, safe, and professionally cared for.

Communication is not limited to words. A therapist communicates through tone of voice, choice of words, facial expression, eye contact, body language, gestures, listening, timing, silence, reactions to feedback, the way instructions are given, and the way boundaries are maintained.

Good communication does not mean talking continuously. In a massage environment, professionalism includes knowing when to speak, what to say, how to say it, how much to say, when to listen, and when to allow the client to enjoy silence.
Communicate enough to understand, reassure, guide and care for the client — but never so much that communication begins to interfere with relaxation.

sections.title: 1. Relevance of Good Client Communication
paragraphs: Good client communication supports comfort, understanding, trust, clarity, safety, relaxation, difficult situations, and the Zura Spa brand.

sections.title: Client Comfort
paragraphs: A client should feel comfortable communicating if pressure is too strong or too light, an area is painful, they are too cold or too warm, their position is uncomfortable, they need the therapist to stop, they have a preference, or they need clarification.
A therapist who creates a comfortable communication environment makes it easier for the client to receive the right experience.

sections.title: Understanding Client Needs
paragraphs: Therapists cannot assume that every client wants the same pressure, massage style, level of conversation, areas of focus, room temperature, positioning, or pace. Communication helps the therapist understand the individual client.

sections.title: Building Trust
paragraphs: Clients relax more easily when they feel that the therapist listens, responds appropriately, respects boundaries, explains necessary actions, and does not dismiss concerns. Trust is created through consistent small interactions.

sections.title: Preventing Misunderstandings
paragraphs: Clear communication reduces confusion regarding what the therapist is about to do, how the client should position themselves, what areas will be worked on, pressure, draping, turning over, session expectations, and boundaries.

sections.title: Supporting Safety
paragraphs: If the client reports pain, tenderness, injury, dizziness, discomfort, or unusual sensitivity, the therapist must listen and respond appropriately. Ignoring client communication can turn a small issue into a serious problem.

sections.title: Creating Relaxation
paragraphs: Communication should support relaxation rather than compete with it. The therapist should not make the client feel responsible for maintaining conversation throughout the massage.
Sometimes the best communication is a calm check-in followed by silence.

sections.title: Handling Difficult Situations
paragraphs: Professional communication becomes especially important when a client complains, is impatient or unhappy, makes an inappropriate request, a misunderstanding occurs, the therapist needs to enforce a boundary, or an issue needs management attention.

sections.title: Protecting the Zura Spa Brand
paragraphs: The client may judge the entire organization based on the conversation they have with one therapist.
A single inappropriate remark can damage confidence built by reception, management, marketing, other therapists, and the massage itself.
Every therapist therefore speaks as a representative of Zura Spa, not merely as an individual.

sections.title: 2. The Therapist's Communication Mindset
paragraphs: The therapist should think: "My communication should help this client feel comfortable, respected and properly cared for."
Before speaking, therapists should consider: Is it necessary? Is it appropriate? Is it professional? Does it help the client? Is this the right time to say it?
Good communication should generally be calm, clear, respectful, brief when appropriate, attentive, emotionally composed, and client-focused.
The conversation should support the client's experience rather than satisfy the therapist's need to talk.

sections.title: 3. The Zura Client Communication Procedure
paragraphs: When communicating with clients, therapists should follow this structured approach throughout the session.

sections.title: Step 1 — Welcome Warmly
paragraphs: When meeting the client: acknowledge them promptly, use a calm tone, maintain appropriate eye contact, give a warm composed smile, and speak respectfully.
Example: "Welcome to Zura Spa. How are you today?"
The therapist should appear pleased to receive the client without becoming excessively familiar.

sections.title: Step 2 — Introduce Yourself Where Necessary
paragraphs: Example: "My name is ____. I'll be attending to you today."
For a 4-hands massage, both therapists should be introduced appropriately. This creates clarity and confidence.

sections.title: Step 3 — Confirm the Service
paragraphs: Before beginning, ensure the therapist understands what the client is receiving.
Example: "You're booked for the Premium Massage today, correct?"
Do not allow uncertainty about the service to continue into the massage room.

sections.title: Step 4 — Ask Relevant Questions
paragraphs: Before the massage begins, confirm important information such as areas of pain, areas requiring attention, pressure preference, sensitive areas, and comfort concerns.
Example: "Do you have any pain or area you would like us to pay particular attention to?"
Keep questions relevant. The client should not feel interrogated.

sections.title: Step 5 — Listen Fully
paragraphs: When the client speaks: allow them to finish, do not interrupt unnecessarily, pay attention, clarify where necessary, and remember relevant information.
If the client says their lower back has been painful, the therapist should not ask ten minutes later whether they had any pain.
Listening includes remembering what was communicated.

sections.title: Step 6 — Acknowledge What the Client Said
paragraphs: A simple acknowledgment shows that the therapist understood.
Examples: "Alright, I'll be careful around that area." or "Understood. We'll focus more on the shoulders today."
This gives the client confidence that their request has been heard.

sections.title: Step 7 — Give Clear Instructions
paragraphs: When the client needs to change, lie face down, turn over, adjust position, or move an arm or leg, give simple respectful instructions.
Example: "Please turn onto your back when you're ready." Not: "Turn."
The instruction should never sound like an order being shouted at the client.

sections.title: Step 8 — Explain Before Actions That Affect Privacy or Positioning
paragraphs: Where necessary, tell the client what you are about to do.
Examples: "I'm going to adjust the towel slightly." "I'll help reposition the pillow for your comfort." "When you're ready, please turn onto your back."
Predictability creates trust.

sections.title: Step 9 — Check Comfort at the Beginning
paragraphs: Before settling fully into the massage: "Are you comfortable?"
Check head position, neck, arms, legs, temperature, and draping. Correct discomfort before continuing.

sections.title: Step 10 — Confirm Pressure
paragraphs: After establishing initial pressure: "How is the pressure for you?"
If the client asks for adjustment, adjust. Do not argue with the client's preference.

sections.title: Step 11 — Observe Non-Verbal Communication
paragraphs: Clients do not always say when something is uncomfortable. Observe sudden body tension, pulling away, flinching, changes in breathing, repeated movement, facial expressions, attempts to reposition, and visible discomfort.
When appropriate, ask: "Is that pressure alright?"
A therapist should learn to listen with their eyes as well as their ears.

sections.title: Step 12 — Allow Silence
paragraphs: Once the client's comfort has been established, allow the massage to become peaceful.

Do not continually ask questions such as where the client works, whether they are married, where they live, what they do, what they are doing later, or why they are quiet — unless there is a legitimate professional reason.
Silence is not awkward in a spa. Silence is part of the service.

sections.title: Step 13 — Follow the Client's Communication Level
paragraphs: If the client begins light appropriate conversation, the therapist may respond politely.
But the therapist should not allow the conversation to become excessively personal, emotional, sexual, political, argumentative, gossip-based, or distracting.
The therapist should remain friendly without turning the professional relationship into a friendship during the session.

sections.title: Step 14 — Check In When Necessary
paragraphs: Communication during massage should usually be purposeful.
Appropriate check-ins include: "Is the pressure still comfortable?" "Is this area tender?" "Are you comfortable in this position?"
Avoid asking the same question every few minutes when there is no reason. Excessive checking can itself disturb relaxation.

sections.title: Step 15 — Respond Immediately to Reasonable Requests
paragraphs: If the client says the pressure is too strong, respond: "Certainly. I'll reduce it."
If the client asks for more focus on the shoulders, respond: "Certainly."
If the client says they are cold, take appropriate action rather than acknowledging it and continuing unchanged.
Communication without response is not effective communication.

sections.title: Step 16 — Communicate Transitions
paragraphs: Before significant transitions, communicate where necessary.
Examples: "When you're ready, please turn onto your back." or "I'll adjust the towel before we continue."
Do not suddenly move, expose or reposition the client without appropriate communication.

sections.title: Step 17 — Communicate Professionally With a Co-Therapist
paragraphs: During a 4-hands massage, therapists may occasionally need to communicate. This should be brief, quiet, professional, and necessary.
Avoid holding full conversations across the client. The client should never feel like they are lying in the middle of a staff discussion.

sections.title: Step 18 — Close the Session Professionally
paragraphs: At the end: "Sir/Ma, we have come to the end of your session. We'll step outside while you change."
Afterwards: "How was your session?" Listen to the feedback and respond appropriately.

sections.title: 4. Tone of Voice Standard
paragraphs: The therapist's tone should generally be calm, warm, respectful, clear, and composed.
Avoid sounding aggressive, irritated, sarcastic, mocking, overexcited, flirtatious, dismissive, bored, or condescending.
The same sentence can communicate completely different meanings depending on tone.
Example: "Please turn over." can sound professional when said gently and disrespectful when said impatiently.

sections.title: 5. Facial Expression Standard
paragraphs: Therapists should maintain a warm, composed and professional expression. A pleasant smile when welcoming or interacting with the client is appropriate.

However, the therapist should avoid excessive smiling that may appear flirtatious, laughing unnecessarily, rolling their eyes, frowning at client requests, making faces after a client speaks, looking irritated, smirking, expressing disgust, or exchanging meaningful looks with a co-therapist about the client.
The client's request or body should never become the subject of facial reactions between therapists.

sections.title: 6. Body Language and Gestures
paragraphs: The therapist should communicate professionalism through body language.
Appropriate body language includes open posture, calm movement, appropriate eye contact, standing attentively when listening, gentle gestures, and respecting personal space.

Avoid folding arms while a client is speaking, pointing aggressively, standing over the client intimidatingly, rolling eyes, shaking the head dismissively, constant fidgeting, looking at the phone, looking around while the client is speaking, whispering and laughing with another therapist, or turning away while responding.
The body can contradict words. Saying "I'm listening." while looking at a phone communicates the opposite.

sections.title: 7. Active Listening Standard
paragraphs: A therapist should practise active listening.
Hear — pay attention to what the client says.
Understand — determine what the client actually means.
Clarify — if necessary: "Do you mean the pain is around your lower back?"
Acknowledge — "Understood."
Respond — adjust the service appropriately.
Remember — do not immediately forget what the client communicated.
The standard is: HEAR → UNDERSTAND → ACKNOWLEDGE → RESPOND.

sections.title: 8. Communicating When the Client Complains
paragraphs: A complaint should not immediately become a confrontation.
If a client says the pressure was too hard, do not respond: "But you told me you wanted deep pressure." Instead: "I understand. I'll reduce the pressure immediately."

If the client gives feedback after the session: listen, do not interrupt, clarify where necessary, acknowledge, apologize appropriately where necessary, escalate when required, and do not make unauthorized promises.
The goal is to understand and resolve the concern.

sections.title: 9. Communicating Professional Boundaries
paragraphs: A therapist should be friendly without becoming personally available to the client.
If a client makes an inappropriate request: "I'm sorry, but that is outside our professional service. I can continue with the approved massage service."
If the client continues: repeat the boundary clearly, do not negotiate, do not joke about the request, do not participate, and follow the appropriate escalation process.
Professional boundaries should be clear without being rude, and firm without being aggressive.

sections.title: 10. Confidentiality Standard
paragraphs: What a client communicates during a session should be treated with discretion.

Therapists should not unnecessarily discuss client relationships, client finances, medical information, personal stories, client behaviour, contact details, complaints, or private conversations with other clients, friends, family, unauthorized staff, or social media contacts.
Relevant information may be communicated internally only where necessary for service delivery, safety, management, or proper documentation.
Client trust depends on discretion.

sections.title: 11. What Good Client Communication Looks Like
paragraphs: A therapist meeting the communication standard greets appropriately, smiles warmly, speaks calmly, listens, remembers client requests, gives clear instructions, checks pressure, responds when the client is uncomfortable, allows silence, maintains boundaries, handles complaints maturely, protects confidentiality, and ends the session professionally.

The client should not have to repeat themselves unnecessarily, fight to be heard, feel embarrassed to request an adjustment, tolerate uncomfortable conversation, listen to staff gossip, or defend their preferences.

sections.title: 12. What the Opposite Looks Like
paragraphs: The opposite of the Zura Spa Communication Standard is communication that is rude, dismissive, overfamiliar, intrusive, argumentative, careless, unprofessional, or distracting.

sections.title: Talking Too Much
paragraphs: The therapist talks throughout the massage and prevents the client from relaxing. The session becomes a conversation rather than a wellness experience.

sections.title: Talking About Yourself Constantly
paragraphs: The therapist discusses their relationship, family, money problems, workplace frustration, personal plans, or private issues. The client becomes an audience for the therapist rather than the person receiving care.

sections.title: Asking Intrusive Questions
paragraphs: Examples include unnecessary questions about relationships, sexual life, income, personal finances, where the client lives, or private family matters.
This may make the client uncomfortable or suspicious of the therapist's intentions.

sections.title: Gossiping
paragraphs: The therapist discusses another client, another therapist, management, reception, or workplace conflict.
This tells the client: "If they talk about other people to me, they may also talk about me."

sections.title: Arguing
paragraphs: The therapist feels the need to prove that they are right. This converts feedback into conflict.

sections.title: Dismissing the Client
paragraphs: Examples: "That's normal." "It's not that painful." "Just relax." "Nobody else complains."
Such responses tell the client that their experience does not matter.

sections.title: Ignoring Non-Verbal Discomfort
paragraphs: The client repeatedly flinches or moves, but the therapist continues without checking.

sections.title: Excessive Familiarity
paragraphs: The therapist flirts, uses suggestive language, gives inappropriate compliments, makes sexual jokes, requests unnecessary personal information, or tries to build a private relationship with the client.
Professional warmth should never become inappropriate familiarity.

sections.title: Cold or Unfriendly Communication
paragraphs: A therapist may barely greet, avoid eye contact, give one-word responses, speak as though irritated, or issue commands instead of requests.
Professionalism should not feel emotionally cold.

sections.title: 13. Why Zura Spa Will Not Tolerate Poor Client Communication
paragraphs: Poor communication cannot be dismissed as "That's just her personality," "She's naturally quiet," or "He talks a lot." Once communication begins affecting the client, it becomes a service-standard issue.

Zura Spa will not normalize rudeness, gossip, arguing with clients, ignoring client discomfort, intrusive questions, sexual or inappropriate conversation, excessive familiarity, disclosure of confidential client information, repeated failure to listen, or communication that makes clients feel unsafe or disrespected.
A technically good massage cannot completely compensate for a therapist who makes the client uncomfortable through conversation or behaviour.

sections.title: 14. Impact of Poor Communication on the Client
paragraphs: Poor communication may cause the client to feel disrespected, feel unheard, feel unsafe, become uncomfortable communicating pain, tolerate wrong pressure instead of speaking, lose trust, become unable to relax, request another therapist, end the session early, complain, avoid returning, leave a negative review, or discourage others from visiting.
The therapist may think: "It was just something I said." The client may remember it as: "That was how Zura Spa treated me."

sections.title: 15. Impact on the Team
paragraphs: Poor client communication does not affect only the therapist involved.

sections.title: It Creates Complaints Others Must Handle
paragraphs: A careless comment made in the treatment room may later require reception involvement, supervisor involvement, management intervention, service recovery, refund discussions, or client follow-up.
A few unnecessary words can create work for several other people.

sections.title: It Damages Trust in Other Therapists
paragraphs: A client who has one poor experience may become suspicious of the next therapist. The next therapist must now rebuild trust they did not personally damage.

sections.title: It Can Affect Co-Therapists
paragraphs: During a 4-hands massage, if one therapist talks excessively, makes inappropriate jokes, argues with the client, or uses disrespectful language, both therapists become associated with the experience.

sections.title: It Creates an Unprofessional Culture
paragraphs: If gossip, oversharing or inappropriate conversations are tolerated, other therapists may begin doing the same. Eventually, inappropriate behaviour becomes normalized.

sections.title: It Creates Internal Conflict
paragraphs: If therapists discuss colleagues or management with clients, information can return to the team and create distrust, arguments, division, and resentment.
Internal matters should be handled internally.

sections.title: It Damages the Shared Brand
paragraphs: Clients rarely say "One therapist communicates poorly." They may simply say "Zura Spa is unprofessional." Everyone therefore carries part of the consequences.

sections.title: 16. Impact of Good Communication on the Team
paragraphs: Good communication reduces complaints, makes handovers easier, builds client confidence, supports co-therapist coordination, makes difficult situations easier to resolve, protects confidentiality, creates a calmer working environment, strengthens the Zura Spa brand, and makes clients more comfortable returning to different therapists.
When every therapist communicates professionally, clients experience one brand standard instead of different personalities competing with the brand.

sections.title: 18. What Therapists Should Not Do
list: Comment unnecessarily on the client's body.
Request personal contact information without a legitimate business reason.
Continue pressure after the client asks for reduction.
Roll eyes at a client request.
Whisper about the client with another therapist.
Speak across the client unnecessarily during 4-hands massage.
Carry workplace anger into client interaction.
Allow personal emotions to determine how a client is treated.
Continue an inappropriate discussion simply because the client initiated it.

sections.title: 19. Communication Correction and Accountability
paragraphs: At Zura Spa: An awkward statement + accepting correction = learning opportunity. Misunderstanding a client + clarifying and correcting = professional recovery. Client feedback + changed behaviour = growth.

But: Repeated rude communication = performance concern. Repeated gossip with clients = serious professionalism concern. Repeated inappropriate or sexual conversation = disciplinary concern. Breaching client confidentiality = serious disciplinary concern.

The expectation is not that therapists must speak perfectly at all times. The expectation is respect, professional judgment, self-control, appropriate boundaries, and willingness to correct poor communication.

sections.title: 20. Communication During Each Stage of the Client Experience
paragraphs: Before the massage: WELCOME → LISTEN → ASSESS → CONFIRM → EXPLAIN.
Massage start: POSITION → CHECK COMFORT → COMMUNICATE → BEGIN → CONFIRM PRESSURE.
During massage: OBSERVE → LISTEN → CHECK WHEN NECESSARY → ADJUST → ALLOW SILENCE.
During transitions: INFORM → PROTECT PRIVACY → POSITION → CONFIRM COMFORT → CONTINUE.
When there is a problem: LISTEN → STAY CALM → CLARIFY → RESPOND → ESCALATE IF NECESSARY.
Massage end: CLOSE → ALLOW → CHECK → LISTEN → RECEIVE FEEDBACK → THANK → GUIDE.

sections.title: 21. The Zura Spa Communication Standard
paragraphs: WELCOME → LISTEN → UNDERSTAND → COMMUNICATE → OBSERVE → RESPOND → RESPECT → PROTECT

Every therapist should regularly ask: Am I speaking respectfully? Am I actually listening? Does the client feel comfortable speaking to me? Am I talking more than necessary? Does this conversation support relaxation? Am I maintaining professional boundaries? Would I be comfortable if management heard this conversation? Would I be comfortable if this client repeated my words publicly as something a Zura Spa therapist said?
That final question is especially important. If the answer is NO, it probably should not be said.
BE WARM, BUT PROFESSIONAL. Create connection without becoming overly familiar.
BE FRIENDLY, BUT RESPECTFUL. Make clients feel welcome without crossing boundaries.
BE CONFIDENT, BUT HUMBLE. Guide the experience while remaining responsive to the client.
SPEAK WHEN NECESSARY, BUT VALUE SILENCE. The client did not come to entertain the therapist.
LISTEN BEFORE RESPONDING. Understanding comes before explanation.
OBSERVE WHAT THE CLIENT DOES NOT SAY. Body language is also communication.
RESPOND, DON'T JUST ACKNOWLEDGE. If the client communicates discomfort, take appropriate action.

At Zura Spa, good communication is not measured by how much the therapist says. It is measured by whether the client leaves feeling: "My therapist listened to me." "I could communicate comfortably." "My preferences were respected." "I was treated professionally." "I felt safe and properly cared for."
WE DON'T JUST SPEAK TO CLIENTS — WE COMMUNICATE WITH CARE. LISTEN. UNDERSTAND. RESPOND. RESPECT. PROTECT THE EXPERIENCE.

remember: Good communication is measured by whether the client felt heard, respected, and properly cared for — not by how much you said.
